conventions.convention: KL is directional: D(P‖Q) is infinite when P is not absolutely continuous with respect to Q. Otherwise AC supplies a finite nonnegative density representative; log density is set to zero where the density vanishes, and 0 log 0 = 0. The negative integral is finite.
Total variation is sup over measurable events of |P(A) − Q(A)|, with values in [0,1]; Pinsker has the factor D(P‖Q)/2 under the square root.
Mutual information uses a uniform prior on {1,…,M}, M ≥ 2, mixture M⁻¹ΣP_j, and natural logarithms.
Finite-product KL additivity assumes AC and n ≥ 1, with factors indexed by i < n on the finite product sigma-algebra. Infinite summands produce an infinite sum.

Sparse packing uses natural d,k with 1 ≤ k ≤ d/2, m = floor(d/k), r = floor(k/4), and zero-based block positions. Natural counts appearing in real expressions are transported through the canonical embedding.
Estimators are arbitrary measurable probability kernels; squared-loss risks are nonnegative iterated integrals and may be infinite. Minimax bounds do not assert existence of a minimizing rule.

Fano uses pairwise target distance at least Δ > 0 in a metric Borel action space, a uniform finite hypothesis experiment, and a probability reference law Q. An infinite reference KL average gives the vacuous lower bound −∞.
The Gaussian location KL formula assumes AC and strictly positive common scale τ; zero-variance Gaussian laws are outside its statement.

load_bearing.statement: If P is not absolutely continuous with respect to Q, D(P‖Q) = +∞. Otherwise, assuming AC, D(P‖Q) = ∫ℓ dP = ∫r log r dQ, where r = dP/dQ, ℓ is zero on {r = 0}, and 0 log 0 = 0; the negative part is finite.
Assume AC. For n ≥ 1 and probability measures P_i,Q_i on measurable spaces indexed by i < n, D(⊗P_i‖⊗Q_i) = ΣD(P_i‖Q_i), where a sum with an infinite term is +∞.
Assume AC. For probability measures P,Q on one measurable space, with TV(P,Q) = sup_A |P(A) − Q(A)|, TV(P,Q) ≤ √(D(P‖Q)/2).

For M ≥ 2 sample laws and targets in a metric Borel space separated by at least Δ > 0, define K_Q = M⁻¹ΣD(P_j‖Q) for a probability reference Q. Every randomized estimator's uniform average and maximum squared-metric risks are at least (Δ²/4)(1 − (K_Q + log 2)/log M); the same holds for minimax risk. Infinite K_Q gives a vacuous bound.
Assume AC and let a,b be real and τ > 0. D(N(a,τ²)‖N(b,τ²)) = (a − b)²/(2τ²).

For natural 1 ≤ k ≤ d/2, m = floor(d/k) and r = floor(k/4), there is C ⊆ [m]^k with distinct-word Hamming distances greater than r and log|C| ≥ (k/1024)log(ed/k). The block vectors have exactly k ones and pairwise squared Euclidean distances greater than k/2.
For a two-point experiment, scalar targets t_0 < t_1 with gap Δ, and any randomized real-valued estimator K, max_j R_j(K) ≥ (Δ²/8)(1 − TV(P_0,P_1)); minimax risk obeys the same bound.
For a uniform index J on {1,…,M}, M ≥ 2, conditional observation laws P_j and mixture P̄ = M⁻¹ΣP_j, define I(J;X) = M⁻¹ΣD(P_j‖P̄).

For d ≥ 1, a > 0, targets aω indexed by ω ∈ {0,1}^d, squared Euclidean loss, and largest neighboring-law total variation v, every randomized estimator has maximum risk at least a²d(1 − v)/8; minimax risk obeys the same bound.
